lead: Every AC circuit at one fixed frequency can be solved with the DC toolkit you already know — mesh, nodal, Thevenin, superposition — once each element is written as an impedance and each source and answer as a phasor. The method skips the switching transient and keeps only the response that survives: the steady state. Electricity boards, motor designers and anyone holding a clamp meter work this way, because at 50 Hz the transient is over in milliseconds.
prereq: You need: phasors and impedance from 3.2 and 3.3, plus mesh, nodal and Thevenin analysis from Unit 2.

blocks.text: The method rests on one fact: at a single frequency ω, every voltage and current in a linear circuit is a sinusoid of that same frequency. Only two numbers change from point to point — magnitude and phase. A phasor carries exactly those two numbers, and an impedance carries how each element scales and shifts them.
So the circuit becomes a complex-number circuit at ω. Kirchhoff's laws are untouched: they hold at every instant, so they also hold for the phasors.

items: Write every source as a phasor V = V∠φ, with φ measured against your chosen reference.
Replace each element by its impedance: R stays R, L becomes jωL, C becomes 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC).
Solve with mesh analysis, nodal analysis or any network theorem, using ordinary complex arithmetic.

Convert the complex answer back: I = |I|∠ψ means i(t) = √2|I| cos(ωt + ψ) when |I| is RMS. Use the same reference as the source: if v(t) = √2|V| cos(ωt + φ) then i(t) = √2|I| cos(ωt + ψ); if the source is written with sin, write the answer with sin.

blocks.text: Keep magnitudes as RMS. Then |V| reads the same as a voltmeter and |I| the same as an ammeter. A supply called 230 V means 230 V RMS, whose peak is 230√2 = 325 V; the √2 appears only when you write the time function.
Z = R + jX,  X = ωL − 1/(ωC),  I = V/Z,  |Z| = √(R² + X²),  θ = tan⁻¹(X/R)
blocks.where: Z is impedance in Ω; R is resistance in Ω; X is net reactance in Ω; ω is angular frequency in rad/s; L is inductance in H; C is capacitance in F; V and I are RMS phasors in V and A; θ is the impedance angle in degrees. Because I = V/Z, the current angle = (angle of V) − θ.

blocks.text: In a series circuit one current flows through all three elements, so you find I first and then multiply by each impedance. The voltages add as phasors, not as numbers.

The sign of θ tells you the story. If X > 0 the circuit is inductive and the current lags the source. If X < 0 the circuit is capacitive and the current leads the source. X = 0 is series resonance, which belongs to Unit 4; there Z = R and the current is largest and in phase.

Two element voltages can each be bigger than the source. Near resonance X_L and X_C are large and nearly equal, so V_L and V_C are large and nearly opposite. Their phasor difference V_L − V_C is small, and that small difference combined with V_R rebuilds the source exactly. A capacitor in a tuned filter can read 338 V while the supply is 230 V, which is why such circuits are handled with care.

sections.h3: Parallel case, real coils, and the Laplace check

blocks.text: In parallel, admittances add: Y = 1/R + jωC + 1/(jωL), and Z = 1/Y. Series-parallel combinations reduce by the same rules as resistors, provided you never drop the j.

Parallel check: R = 30 Ω in parallel with L = 0.1 H at ω = 314.16 rad/s. X_L = 31.42 Ω, so Z = (30 × j31.42)/(30 + j31.42) = 15.69 + j14.99 Ω, that is 21.70 Ω at 43.7°. Adding admittances gives the same: Y = 0.0333 − j0.0318 S.

A practical coil is never pure inductance; the winding has resistance. Model it as one impedance R + jωL with R the measured DC resistance. Its angle is then less than 90°, and ignoring that resistance is a common source of wrong answers in power-factor problems.

Unit 5 solves the same circuit with the Laplace transform. Its partial-fraction answer has a transient that decays like e^(−t/τ) plus a steady sinusoid. As t → ∞ the transient vanishes and only the phasor answer remains. Both roads agree; the phasor road is shorter when the steady state is all you want.

figure.caption: The steady-state pipeline for the worked example. Notice that the complex current 5.31∠22.5° A is not the answer until it is turned back into a sine (or cosine, matching the source) with a phase.

spec.aria: A four-step pipeline: a sine source, the three element impedances, a mesh or nodal solution, a complex current 5.31∠22.5° A, and finally the time-domain current 7.51 sin(314.16t + 22.5°) A.

examples.question: A series RLC circuit has R = 40 Ω, L = 0.15 H and C = 50 µF. The source is v(t) = 230√2 sin(314.16t) V. Find i(t) and the RMS voltages across R, L and C, and check that the element voltages rebuild the source.
steps: ω = 314.16 rad/s. The source as an RMS phasor is V = 230∠0° V (peak 230√2 = 325.3 V).
Net reactance X = X_L − X_C = 47.12 − 63.66 = −16.54 Ω. Negative, so the circuit is capacitive.
The current angle is 0 − (−22.5°) = +22.5°, so the current leads the source: i(t) = 7.51 sin(314.16t + 22.5°) A.
V_R = I R = 5.31 × 40 = 212.5 V, in phase with I.
Magnitude check: √(212.5² + (250.4 − 338.3)²) = √(45156 + 7726) = √52882 = 230.0 V, the source. V_L and V_C individually exceed 230 V but nearly cancel.
examples.check:
import math
w = 314.16
L = 0.15
C = 50e-6
R = 40.0
V = 230.0
XL = w * L
XC = 1 / (w * C)
X = XL - XC
Z = math.hypot(R, X)
th = math.degrees(math.atan2(X, R))
I = V / Z
Ipk = I * math.sqrt(2)
VR = I * R
VL = I * XL
VC = I * XC
src = math.hypot(VR, VL - VC)
print(round(XL, 2))
print(round(XC, 2))
print(round(X, 2))
print(round(Z, 2))
print(round(th, 1))
print(round(I, 2))
print(round(Ipk, 2))
print(round(VR, 1))
print(round(VL, 1))
print(round(VC, 1))
print(round(src, 1))

traps: Stopping at Z or I in complex form. The examiner wants the time function with its phase; a bare 5.31∠22.5° A can lose half the marks.

Subtracting V_L from V_C as if the two were in phase. They are 180° apart, so they oppose as phasors; written as 250.4 − 338.3 they only look like a subtraction because both are taken along the same axis.
Mixing peak and RMS. Phasors are kept in RMS so they match meter readings, and √2 is applied only when writing i(t). Mixing the two scales gives answers wrong by 41%.
Treating a real coil as pure jωL. Its winding resistance must sit in the same impedance, so the coil angle is below 90°.
Reversing lead and lag. Check the sign: X > 0 means inductive and the current lags; X < 0 means capacitive and the current leads.

quiz.q: Write the impedance of L and of C at angular frequency ω, with magnitude and angle.
quiz.a: Z_L = jωL, magnitude ωL, angle +90°. Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), magnitude 1/(ωC), angle −90°.

quiz.q: List the four steps of steady-state AC analysis.
quiz.a: Sources to phasors; elements to impedances; solve by mesh, nodal or a theorem with complex arithmetic; convert the complex result back to a time function.

quiz.q: In a series RLC circuit, how can the voltage across C be larger than the source voltage?
quiz.a: Near resonance X_C is large, so V_C = I X_C is large. But V_C is 90° behind the current and V_L is 90° ahead, so they are 180° apart and their phasor difference is small. That small difference plus V_R equals the source.

quiz.q: A series circuit has R = 20 Ω and X = −20 Ω. Does the current lead or lag, and by how much?
quiz.a: θ = tan⁻¹(−20/20) = −45°, so Z = 28.28∠−45° Ω. The circuit is capacitive and the current leads the source by 45°.

quiz.q: A series RL circuit has R = 60 Ω and L = 0.2 H, fed by v(t) = 230√2 sin(314.16t) V. Find i(t).
R = 30 Ω in parallel with L = 0.1 H at ω = 314.16 rad/s. Find Z in rectangular and polar form.
In a series RLC circuit the current leads the source and V_C > V_L. Is the frequency above or below resonance? Justify.
quiz.a: Below resonance. There X_C > X_L, so X = X_L − X_C is negative and the circuit is capacitive. A capacitive series circuit gives leading current, and V_C = I X_C exceeds V_L = I X_L since the same current flows through both.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators such as ngspice and LTspice run exactly this calculation at every frequency point of an AC sweep: build the complex matrix, solve it, print magnitude and phase. The same complex-matrix idea scales up to power-flow studies, where thousands of buses at 50 Hz are solved together to decide which generator supplies whom. Search for "phasor-domain nodal analysis", "AC sweep analysis" and "Newton-Raphson power flow" to see the industrial version.
